summary: Technical deep dive on supporting ultra-long contexts (>=128k tokens) for Sable Bios' R&D assistant use case. Covered chunking, attention window strategies, persistent KV caching, eviction policies, tradeoffs of aggressive quantization for throughput, and constraints for on-prem/VPC deployment. Agreed to run an initial PoC benchmark and share security docs.
transcript:
Meeting Header:
- Date/Time: 2026-04-12 15:00 PDT
- Duration: 82 minutes
- Platform: Zoom
- Recording: yes (auto)
- Participants: Maya Patel, Evan Zhang, Priya Rao (Redwood); Dr. Lina Ortega, Rajiv Menon, Sophie Chen, Carlos Ruiz, Jun Park (Sable)

Summary:
- See topics above; main ask is to support live R&D assistant workflows where users ingest entire experiment logs (100k-300k tokens) and run interactive refinement queries under 1.2s tail latency for short queries. Sable cares about cost (dedicated vs hosted), data residency, and persistent KV to avoid re-encoding common prefixes.

Topics: 128k+ context design, chunking, attention optimizations, persistent KV, eviction policies, quantization strategy, VPC/on-prem constraints, benchmarking approach.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we know you all are busy, so Evan and I will run through some design patterns for long context and then jump into specifics for your infra. Lina, want to start with a quick use case recap?
[00:18] Dr. Lina Ortega: yeah thanks, basically researchers will upload full experiment logs, notebooks, and design notes — often multiple runs — we want the assistant to answer comparitive questions across experiments, and recall past parameters. so context size routinely hits 150k to 250k tokens.
[00:33] Evan Zhang: ok so the two big axes we need to optimize for are latency for the interactive query path and unit cost for storing and reusing prefixes. if every read re-tokenizes everything it's expensive.
[00:44] Rajiv Menon: quick question, we currently use an internal GPU cluster (A100 + mix of H100 dev nodes), and on-prem strict networking (no outbound except via proxy). is that going to block a Redwood Private deployment?
[00:58] Maya Patel: not at all, we do Private with a customer-managed control plane and can run the runtime in your VPC / on-prem with our agent. the only extra is KMS/HSM integration for keys and we have patterns for air-gapped setups. Evan will cover infra reqs.
[01:12] Evan Zhang: right, for 128k+ we generally recommend a hybrid strategy: 1) chunk the document into semantically coherent segments (chapter / experiment boundaries), 2) build a persistent KV cache of chunk embeddings and token-level KV so we can attach cached prefixes to low-latency queries, and 3) have an eviction policy that favors recently accessed and high-similarity chunks.
[01:34] Sophie Chen: when you say "token-level KV" do you mean keeping the full KV cache of transformer keys/values for each chunk in GPU memory? that sounds huge.
[01:44] Evan Zhang: great point — there are two layers. for warm-starts we keep chunk embeddings and a compact provenance pointer (metadata + start token). then for very hot prefixes we materialize the KV cache on GPU. we do not keep full materialized KV for all chunks; that's only for the hottest ones.
[02:05] Jun Park: and how do you measure hottest? LRU? freq? weighted recency?
[02:12] Evan Zhang: we use a combination — recency-weighted frequency with an estimated cost to reload the KV (that cost is proportional to chunk length and tokenize rate). we observed better hit rates when using sim-based hotness (how often the chunk matches queries).
[02:28] Dr. Lina Ortega: what's the expected memory footprint for, say, 150k of tokens split into 1k token chunks with hotset of 25 chunks?
[02:38] Evan Zhang: ballpark: a single 1k chunk's KV for a 70B model is around 80-110MB depending on kv-precision. so 25 chunks is ~2-3GB of GPU RAM to keep hot; not crazy. but if you try to keep entire 150 chunks materialized it's 12-16GB, which is more costly.
[02:58] Rajiv Menon: ok that seems feasible on H100 nodes we have. what about streaming / append workflows where researchers add new logs continuously? do you rebuild chunks incrementally?
[03:09] Maya Patel: yes incremental chunking is key — we support append pipelines: new text is tokenized, diffed to detect boundary shifts, we only re-embed affected chunks, and we can asynchronously pre-warm the KV for newly hot chunks.
[03:24] Carlos Ruiz: security question — if KV contains sensitive values, do you encrypt KV on disk and in-transit? and what about strict audit logging?
[03:33] Priya Rao: KV on disk is encrypted using customer KMS keys; in-memory KV is ephemeral and never written back unless persisted to encrypted store. we also emit audit events for KV materialization and cache hits tied to token-level traces (redacted). we can provide SOC2 artefacts.
[03:52] Dr. Lina Ortega: let's talk quantization — we need higher throughput since users run many queries. what's the trade off with aggressive 4-bit quant?
[04:01] Evan Zhang: 4-bit quant (GPTQ-style) gets you big memory and throughput wins, often 2-3x faster than int8 for decode in our runtime given kernel optimizations, but you can see small generative quality regressions in adversarial prompt slices — especially for instruction-following. our suggestion: use mixed strategy — int8 for safety-critical cores and 4-bit for batch offline rerank jobs.
[04:27] Sophie Chen: can you run INT4 for everything and fallback when hallucinations are detected?
[04:33] Evan Zhang: you can, but detection adds complexity. better approach: route short interactive queries to an int8 or fp16 low-latency model and heavy long-context reasoning to a quantized model with a quality-check A/B sampler. we also support auto-fallback policies in the router.
[04:51] Jun Park: this router — is it part of Redwood Private runtime? how configurable?
[04:56] Maya Patel: yes it's part of the routing layer; rules can be by latency, cost, region, model quality tag, or headers. you can add canary or A/B logic and fallback on error or latency SLO misses.
[05:08] [05:08] Speaker 1: [inaudible] can you show a sample eviction policy?
[05:12] Evan Zhang: sure, here's a simple policy we use: score_chunk = alpha * recency_score + beta * frequency_score - gamma * reload_cost. eviction picks lowest score. alpha/beta/gamma are tunables. we also tag chunks as "pinned" if they're globally important to a project.
[05:33] Rajiv Menon: makes sense. what about multi-tenant isolation? we want per-project pinned caches and quotas.
[05:40] Priya Rao: we have namespace-level cache separation and quotas for cached memory. dedicated pools for enterprise customers give isolated GPU pools and configurable limits.
[05:48] Dr. Lina Ortega: benchmarking — what should we run to validate 1) average tail latency for short queries and 2) throughput for long-batch analytic jobs?
[05:58] Evan Zhang: run two benchmarks: a microbench for 50-100k short queries against hot cache to measure p99/p50, and a macro benchmark where you replay 200-300 full long-context reads to exercise cold cache population, eviction churn, and end-to-end cost. include synthetic adversarial prompts to measure hallucination rate when running 4-bit quant.
[06:20] [06:20] Sophie Chen: any recommended numbers to expect on H100 for a 40B model with mixed quant and hot cache?
[06:26] Evan Zhang: for 40B on H100 with hotset materialized and int8 decode you can hit sub-300ms median for short queries; p99 depends on network and prewarm but expect 600-900ms in a well tuned stack. for 4-bit batches throughput increases 2-3x but p99 can widen if fallback logic triggers.
[06:46] Dr. Lina Ortega: we assume many researchers will do multi-turn followups; is there an efficient way to keep context without reloading everything?
[06:54] Evan Zhang: yes session affinity with incremental KV append — when a session is active we keep its hotset pinned on the serving node and stream small diffs. this reduces token cost for repeated queries. if session goes idle it falls back to the persistent store and may be evicted.
[07:10] Jun Park: if we run Private on-prem, how is autoscaling handled? we have a variable workload and can't always add more expensive GPUs.
[07:19] Maya Patel: our Dedicated and Private runtimes support both scale-up (add more GPUs to pool) and scale-out with cost-aware routing. you can configure minimum hot capacity and burst policies, and we support pre-warming nodes for planned heavy runs.
[07:34] Carlos Ruiz: for audits we need full request traces and who accessed what. how granular are logs?
[07:40] Priya Rao: we log token-level request ids, model version, KV-chunk ids referenced (redacted if necessary), user id, and route decisions. logs can be shipped to your SIEM and retention is configurable.
[07:56] Dr. Lina Ortega: ok I want to deep-dive quantization numbers later, can Evan share benchmarks?
[08:02] Evan Zhang: yes we'll share our quant benchmark sheet; it includes perplexity deltas, downstream task accuracy and throughput for fp16/int8/4-bit variants across 7B/40B/70B families.
[08:15] Sophie Chen: curious on costs — if we keep, say, 10 pinned chunks per active project and run 20 concurrent sessions, what's cost delta vs naive decoding?
[08:25] Evan Zhang: very rough: caching hot chunks reduces per-token compute by about 30-50% depending on prompt distribution. exact numbers depend on your token distribution; we'll run your sample set through the harness.
[08:38] [08:38] Speaker 2 (jun): when eviction happens during a long job, do you see tail spikes?
[08:42] Evan Zhang: yes if a required chunk is evicted and needs re-materialization mid-request you'll see a spike; we mitigate with prefetching heuristics and soft-reservation of next-n chunks.
[08:55] Dr. Lina Ortega: let's talk datastore choices for persistent KV — SSD vs NVMe vs in-memory DB?
[09:02] Evan Zhang: big difference: NVMe with tuned concurrent reads gives best balance for rehydrate latency. an in-memory store (RAM-backed, e.g., Redis on big nodes) gives best latency but at huge cost. we prefer NVMe backed with local caching on the serving node.
[09:16] Rajiv Menon: do you use any compression for on-disk KV?
[09:20] Evan Zhang: yes we compress serialized KV with lightweight codecs; that cuts storage ~2-3x with small CPU overhead on rehydrate.
[09:28] Jun Park: what about dedupe across chunks? many experiments have the same boilerplate methods section. can we dedupe to reduce storage?
[09:35] Evan Zhang: absolutely — we do content fingerprinting and canonicalization to merge duplicate chunks and maintain reference counts. it reduces both disk storage and KV duplication.
[09:45] Sophie Chen: question around multi-model fallback — can Redwood route between different model size/precision for the same query?
[09:52] Maya Patel: yes route-by-policy is core. Example: short question -> 13B int8, long reasoning -> 70B 4-bit, fallback to 40B int8 if 70B node saturated.
[10:05] Dr. Lina Ortega: on the PoC, we want to see cold-start behavior and warm behavior. can Redwood run both in our env?
[10:12] Maya Patel: yes we can run the harness in your VPC, collect logs and key metrics, and then return a results deck. we'll need a small dataset, sample queries, and access to a representative node with NVMe and GPU.
[10:25] [10:25] Carlos Ruiz: what about key management? KMS integration details for HSM keys?
[10:30] Priya Rao: we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure KeyVault, and customer HSMs via PKCS11. keys never leave customer control in Private mode.
[10:39] Rajiv Menon: connectivity — our cluster is behind strict egress, is the control plane agent pull-based?
[10:45] Evan Zhang: the agent can be configured pull-based and only initiate outbound on customer allowed endpoints. we also support offline bundles for fully air-gapped deployments.
[10:57] Dr. Lina Ortega: sample latency targets we care about: 95% of short queries under 600ms, 99% under 1.2s. is that achievable?
[11:06] Evan Zhang: yes with pinned hotset and local NVMe rehydrate we can get p95 < 400-600ms and p99 near your 1.2s goal depending on network. we'll need to tune tokenization and routing.
[11:20] Sophie Chen: what about observability — what dashboards do you provide?
[11:24] Priya Rao: per-route latency, per-token cost, cache hit rates, model-version rollout dashboards, trace views for request path with token counts, and alerting integrations.
[11:36] [11:36] Speaker 3: quick interjection, we need to estimate the engineering lift for the PoC on our side.
[11:41] Maya Patel: typical PoC needs: 1 infra engineer to provision nodes + network rules, 1 ML engineer to provide dataset and quality evals, and a product owner for acceptance. Redwood SE will run the harness and help with tuning. timeline 3-4 weeks.
[11:58] Dr. Lina Ortega: sounds good. can we also test quantized fine-tuning (QLoRA style) for our domain data?
[12:05] Evan Zhang: we support QLoRA-style adapters for domain tuning; note training requires different infra and persisting quantized checkpoints has caveats — we can discuss in a separate session.
[12:16] Jun Park: are there known gotchas with tokenization across different model families when chunking?
[12:22] Evan Zhang: yes tokenization mismatch can shift chunk boundaries. we normalize using model tokenizer and store token-aligned offsets, and we recommend using a single tokenizer family per project.
[12:33] Sophie Chen: any tips for prompt engineering to reduce re-materialization?
[12:37] Evan Zhang: yes avoid re-sending long redundant context in every query; instead reference chunk ids and include minimal selector prompts. we also support structured context inputs (e.g., metadata tags) to guide retrieval.
[12:50] [12:50] Rajiv Menon: about costs, do you support committed capacity for Private?
[12:54] Maya Patel: yes Dedicated/Private have reserved capacity contracts with discounts and burst options. we'll include pricing scenarios in the scoping doc.
[13:03] Dr. Lina Ortega: great. can we get an example of the harness output after you run it on our sample set?
[13:09] Evan Zhang: yes we'll provide a deck with p50/p95/p99, cost per 1k tokens, cache hit rate, fallback rate, and quality metrics.
[13:20] Sophie Chen: make sure you include per-token cost breakdown — compute, storage, network.
[13:24] Priya Rao: will do.
[13:28] [13:28] Maya Patel: ok let's recap next steps and owners quickly.
[13:31] Maya Patel: next steps: 1) Redwood to send PoC scoping and pricing (Maya) by 2026-04-16, 2) Redwood SE to share benchmark harness and quant benchmarks (Evan) by 2026-04-15, 3) Sable to provide sample dataset and access plan (Lina/Rajiv) by 2026-04-20, 4) security docs to Carlos (Priya) by 2026-04-16.
[13:55] Dr. Lina Ortega: yes we'll try to get dataset ready earlier.
[14:01] Sophie Chen: anything else on the roadmap?
[14:04] Maya Patel: we'll also propose an initial PoC scope for 3-4 weeks and a success criteria doc — measure p99 latency, cache hit rate > 60% after warm, and quality delta < 3% for critical tasks.
[14:18] [14:18] Rajiv Menon: thanks everyone.
[14:20] Maya Patel: thanks all — we'll follow up with artifacts.
